reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: Progressive overinflation of one pulmonary lobe due to a check-valve mechanism that traps air on expiration
The upper and middle lobes, particularly the left upper lobe, are most commonly affected
Often presents in the neonatal period or early infancy with progressive respiratory distress, tachypnoea, and wheeze
The hyperinflated lobe can cause mediastinal shift, compression of adjacent lung, and haemodynamic compromise mimicking a tension pneumothorax
A frequent cause is bronchomalacia or intrinsic/extrinsic bronchial obstruction of the affected lobe, though many cases are idiopathic
Chest radiograph shows a hyperlucent, expanded lobe with compressed adjacent lung and mediastinal displacement, which must not be mistaken for pneumothorax
Symptomatic infants are treated by lobectomy, while mildly affected or asymptomatic older children may be managed conservatively
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital lobar emphysema results from a ball-valve or check-valve obstruction of the bronchus supplying one lobe, so air enters during inspiration but cannot fully escape on expiration, leading to progressive air trapping and overdistension of that lobe. The obstruction may be intrinsic, from deficient or dysplastic bronchial cartilage causing bronchomalacia and collapse, or extrinsic, from vascular or mass compression; in a proportion of cases no cause is identified. The expanding lobe compresses the surrounding normal lung, shifts the mediastinum, and can impair venous return, producing the picture of progressive respiratory and, in severe cases, cardiovascular compromise. The affected lobe is overinflated rather than truly destroyed as in acquired emphysema.
additionalDifferentials: Bronchial foreign body causing air trapping
Bronchogenic cyst causing extrinsic bronchial compression
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph demonstrating a hyperlucent overexpanded lobe with mediastinal shift
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to define the lobe involved and seek a compressing lesion or vessel
Echocardiography to exclude associated cardiac anomalies and vascular compression
Bronchoscopy where an intraluminal or extrinsic obstruction is suspected
Ventilation-perfusion assessment in selected older children
Antenatal ultrasound review, as some cases are detected prenatally
redFlags: Rapidly progressive respiratory distress with mediastinal shift suggesting tension physiology
Cardiovascular compromise from compression of the heart and great veins
Misdiagnosis as pneumothorax leading to inappropriate chest drain insertion
Severe hyperinflation worsening acutely with positive-pressure ventilation
Cyanosis or feeding difficulty from significant lung compression
reference.prognosis: Lobectomy in symptomatic infants is generally curative with a good long-term outcome, as the remaining lung compensates well. Mildly symptomatic or incidentally found cases may remain stable without surgery under observation.
pitfalls: Mistaking the hyperlucent lobe for a pneumothorax and inserting a chest drain
Applying vigorous positive-pressure ventilation, which can distend the affected lobe further
Overlooking an extrinsic compressing lesion or vascular anomaly as the cause
Attributing persistent wheeze to reactive airway disease and missing lobar overinflation
Delaying surgery in a deteriorating infant with progressive mediastinal shift
